title: Complexity in infinite argumentation with structural constraints
abstract: Abstract Argumentation frameworks (AFs) provide a formal setting to analyse many forms of reasoning with conflicting information. Even for finite AFs, practical use is complicated by the computational intractability of many reasoning problems. As such, a number of researchers have explored special classes of AFs, such as those defined by bipartite, acyclic or symmetric finite directed graphs, wherein many reasoning problems become tractable. In many applications, however, infinite AFs are required to adequately capture the structure of reasoning. Recent work has initiated a systematic study of the complexity of reasoning in infinite AFs using tools from computability theory, revealing that many problems in this setting are not even finite-time approximable. This paper investigates how structural constraints—specifically, bipartiteness, acyclicity and symmetry—affect the complexity of reasoning in infinite AFs. We show that in some cases, these constraints suffice to restore finite-time approximability, while in others they do not. Our results reveal the subtle role of structural properties in shaping computational behaviour, and they provide foundational insights for identifying conditions under which reasoning in infinite AFs becomes computationally feasible.

title: Too Smart to Trust? Algorithmic Intelligence and the Erosion of Consumer Autonomy
abstract: As algorithmic intelligence becomes increasingly sophisticated, consumers may perceive not empowerment but erosion of autonomy. This research introduces Algorithmic Autonomy Erosion (AAE) as a distinct psychological mechanism explaining why highly intelligent AI systems can undermine trust. Across three studies a scale development, a controlled experiment, and a large-scale-survey results demonstrate that perceived algorithmic intelligence reduces trust indirectly through heightened autonomy erosion and subsequent psychological reactance. Evidence for a nonlinear effect is mixed. By shifting the focus from performance to perceived authorship displacement, this study advances theory on AI trust and consumer agency.

title: From CNNs to Vision Transformers: A Survey on Addressing Domain Shift and Adaptation Concepts in Medical Image Analysis
abstract: Abstract Medical imaging models increasingly achieve high performance under controlled experimental settings, yet their reliability often degrades when applied across institutions, scanners, imaging protocols, and patient populations. This review examines Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures, together with domain adaptation methods, to address the generalization challenges posed by domain shift in medical imaging. By integrating 160 high-quality studies into a unified analytical framework, the review identifies scenarios in which ViT-based methods offer potential advantages, summarizes effective adaptation techniques, and discusses key obstacles to clinical implementation. The findings show that although ViTs are well suited to capturing global context and long-range dependencies, their reported performance improvements do not imply universal dominance. Their effectiveness depends on dataset characteristics, shift severity, pretraining quality, adaptation strategy, and task type. Adversarial learning, feature alignment, and self-supervised pretraining are identified as effective strategies for reducing cross-domain performance degradation, while CNN–ViT hybrid models offer a practical trade-off between accuracy, robustness, and computational feasibility. Nonetheless, high computational demands, substantial data requirements, interpretability limitations, and the lack of standardized multicenter evaluations continue to hinder widespread clinical use. To address these gaps, the review emphasizes a domain-aware evaluation perspective that distinguishes average task performance from robustness-oriented measures, including cross-domain performance drop, domain-wise variability, worst-domain performance, and calibration under distribution shift. Future research should focus on efficient ViT designs, small-sample adaptation, privacy-preserving frameworks, and robust evaluation protocols that account for cross-domain variability, calibrated uncertainty, workflow integration, regulatory readiness, human oversight, drift monitoring, and controlled model updating in real-world medical imaging environments.

title: Finishing Oltean's Completeness Proof in Lean 4 for Hybrid Logic $L(\forall)$
abstract: We present a machine-checked completeness theorem, in Lean 4, for the hybrid logic $L(\forall)$: propositional modal logic with nominals, the satisfaction-style binder $\forall$, and the box modality. (Machine-checked completeness for basic hybrid logic, without binders, was pioneered by Asta Halkjær From in Isabelle/HOL.) We build on Alex Oltean's 2023 Lean 4 formalization, which mechanized the syntax, semantics, Hilbert-style proof system, and soundness following Blackburn's Hybrid Completeness (1998), but left completeness unfinished. Finishing it requires manufacturing fresh names at two structurally different points, and our central finding is that they call for two different tools. (1) The root witnessed maximal consistent set, built by an extended Lindenbaum construction, needs at each step a nominal fresh for the whole set; the right tool is structural freshness: extend the language so an infinite supply of nominals is reserved by construction. We survey the design space (Oltean's odd/even encoding inside $\mathbb{N}$, the disjoint-sum $N \oplus \mathbb{N}$ parameterization suggested by Bud Mishra, and From's synthetic-completeness frameworks) and explain the encoding we adopt. (2) The witnessed $\Diamond$-successor of a maximal consistent set cannot be obtained this way: its canonical box-reduct provably mentions every nominal, so no reserved name is fresh. Here the right tool is one Oltean chose but left incomplete: an existence-lemma Henkin construction drawing each witness from the predecessor's witnessedness through a fresh state variable; we complete it with a data-carrying witness accumulator and a compactness argument. The theorem $Γ\models φ\to Γ\vdash φ$ is fully formalized: the development is sorry-free, and #print axioms reports only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. We port the development to Lean v4.30.0 / mathlib v4.30.0.

title: Real-time data from a photovoltaic power station in Huicheng District, Huizhou, Guangdong.
abstract: This dataset contains real operational data of a photovoltaic power station located in Huicheng District, Huizhou City, Guangdong Province, China. The dataset covers the time period from June 15, 2026 to June 17, 2026, with a sampling frequency of every hour. The data fields include but are not limited to: environmental temperature and humidity, precipitation, wind speed and direction. This data has been preprocessed by outlier removal and interpolation completion, and can be used for research in photovoltaic power prediction, equipment fault diagnosis, and energy efficiency evaluation.

title: HICE/FA-Hub for Medical Projection-Loss Diagnostics A Residual-Preserving Architecture for Hidden Regime Transitions in Multimodal Biomedical Time Series
abstract: Medical time series rarely observe disease state directly. EEG, ECG/HRV, respiration, laboratory values, imaging, wearable signals, and clinical scores are projections of a latent physiological trajectory, each with its own sampling bias, noise, and information loss. This manuscript presents a conservative HICE/FA-Hub architecture for medical projection-loss diagnostics. HICE contributes the mathematical language of native state, measurement projection, ordered path record, cross-projection residual, and relational two-history comparison. FA-Hub contributes the governance layer: null-model ladders, claim-state ledgers, attribution constraints, and residual preservation. The framework is methodological only. It does not import HLV physical ontology, does not claim that Spiral-Time is a biological mechanism, and does not establish clinical diagnostic performance. The manuscript defines projection-loss functionals, ordered projection-loss records, a hidden-transition score, a HICE-MED0–HICE-MED7 validation ladder, and mandatory null models for real-data studies. A companion synthetic Colab environment is incorporated as a reproducibility demonstrator: it produces latent trajectories, multimodal projections, projectionloss features, null-model scores, figures, SHA-256 manifests, and a claim-state ledger. Its current outputs are interpreted strictly as software debugging and methodological provenance: the synthetic HICE-Med score reaches AUC 0.857, but a single-channel null reaches AUC 1.000 and a time-shuffle null also reaches AUC 0.857, blocking any performance or ordered-history claim. The strongest admissible statement is therefore that HICE/FA-Hub provides a falsifiable architecture for future medical projection-loss studies, not a validated clinical tool.
